\begin{frontmatter}
\title{Masking cannot remove what is inside the region of interest: location-dependent shortcut mitigation across dermoscopy, ultrasound and capsule endoscopy}

\begin{abstract}
Medical image classifiers exploit acquisition artifacts---hair, sonographer calipers, intestinal debris---that
correlate with the diagnosis; the standard defence restricts the model to the region of interest (ROI). This defence
depends on where the artifact sits. In pre-registered traps built from real artifacts in four diseases and three
modalities, masking removes an out-of-ROI shortcut but leaves an in-ROI one largely intact (crossover $+0.15$ to $+0.38$
reversed-test AUROC, all Holm-significant; $+0.25$ on new patients). Moving the \emph{same} real artifact across the ROI
boundary of the \emph{same} images reproduces the effect (location interaction
\input{tables/review2_abstract_transplant}). It holds for five masking implementations, falls continuously with the
artifact--ROI overlap, replicates across encoders, fine-tuning and zero-shot vision--language scores, and grows when
images with contradicted labels are removed. A linear-Gaussian account predicted 84 results registered before they
existed (mean absolute error 0.011 AUROC). On unaltered data the harm hides in subgroups: overall AUROC barely changes,
but masking lowers AUROC on shortcut-conflicting cases, on a patient-disjoint thyroid split and on new patients, and
lowers sensitivity among malignant nodules carrying a caliper for a near-benchmark fine-tuned model, in a subgroup
registered in advance, partly even after re-tuning the threshold. Against a registered criterion, no remedy dominates
masking; the closest, a class-conditional mean constraint on the masked features, removes masking's failure in every
cohort and on every set of conflicting cases, at a cost of 0.02 overall AUROC on one external set. Audits of ROI-masked
models should report artifact location and shortcut-conflicting performance. Code, pre-registrations and results are
public.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
shortcut learning \sep spurious correlation \sep region-of-interest masking \sep artifacts \sep dermoscopy \sep ultrasound \sep capsule endoscopy
\end{keyword}
\end{frontmatter}

\section{Introduction}
Deep classifiers for medical images frequently rely on features that are correlated with the label in the
training distribution but are not evidence of disease \citep{geirhos2020shortcut,degrave2021ai}. In dermoscopy,
surgical skin markings \citep{winkler2019markings} and ruler scale bars \citep{winkler2021scalebars} changed
the melanoma predictions of a market-approved system; in chest radiography, pneumothorax classifiers detect the
chest drain that treats the condition rather than the condition itself
\citep{oakden2020hidden,jimenez2023shortcuts,zech2018variable}. Such correlations are causal in origin---suspicious lesions are
measured and marked, collapsed lungs are drained---so they are present in every retrospectively collected dataset.

The most widely recommended defence is to restrict the classifier to the region of interest (ROI): segment the
lesion or the lungs and discard the rest of the image. The rationale assumes that the shortcut lives in the
background. Rulers, hair, calipers and debris do not respect that assumption. That a mask cannot remove what it keeps
sounds self-evident; its consequences are not. We show that masking makes a model rely \emph{more} on an artifact
inside the ROI, that the resulting harm is hidden in overall metrics but concentrated in the cases a shortcut gets
wrong, that it can be predicted before it is observed, and what to use instead.

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A location law, tested causally.} In traps built from real artifacts in four diseases and three imaging
modalities, masking removes an out-of-ROI shortcut but leaves an in-ROI one largely intact (Holm-significant
crossovers in 4/4 cohorts). Moving the \emph{same} real artifact across the ROI boundary of the \emph{same} images
reproduces the effect, so it is caused by location, not by which images carry artifacts. It holds for five masking
implementations, is graded in the real overlap, replicates across encoders, end-to-end fine-tuning and new patients,
and grows when images with contradicted labels are removed (Sec.~\ref{sec:law}).
\item \textbf{Mechanism and a closed-form account.} Masking retains an in-ROI artifact while removing competing
evidence, so reliance on it grows. A two-parameter linear-Gaussian account states when in-ROI masking harms and
predicted 84 results registered before they existed (Secs.~\ref{sec:mech}, \ref{sec:theory}).
\item \textbf{Clinical consequences on unaltered data.} Masking leaves overall AUROC nearly unchanged but lowers it on
shortcut-conflicting cases of a patient-disjoint thyroid split and of new patients; for a fine-tuned thyroid model near
the published benchmark it lowers sensitivity among malignant nodules carrying a caliper, and part of that loss survives
re-tuning the threshold on the test set (Sec.~\ref{sec:natural}).
\item \textbf{What to use instead.} Against a registered criterion, tested in two rounds on newly generated data, no
remedy dominates masking. The closest, a class-conditional mean constraint on the masked features, removes masking's
in-ROI failure in every cohort and on every set of conflicting cases, at a small overall cost on one external set
(Sec.~\ref{sec:guide}).
\end{enumerate}
Every confirmatory analysis was registered before its results, every reported interval is traced automatically to a
result file, and code, registrations and result files are public.

\section{Related work}
\paragraph{Artifacts as shortcuts} \citet{bissoto2020debiasing} annotated seven artifact types in ISIC images and
showed that debiasing is harder than it looks; \citet{nauta2022uncovering} neutralised coloured calibration patches,
which lie largely outside the lesion, by inpainting and retraining. Hair occlusion degrades classifiers trained on
HAM10000 \citep{wang2024hair}, and adding synthetic dark-corner artifacts helps more than removing real ones
\citep{pewton2024dca}; MaskMedPaint \citep{maskmedpaint} inpaints regions outside the classification-relevant area. In
fetal ultrasound, calipers and on-screen text act as shortcuts even for segmentation \citep{lin2024segshortcut}. In
chest radiography, hospital signals limit generalisation \citep{zech2018variable}, drain shortcuts are documented on
NIH-CXR14 and CheXpert \citep{oakden2020hidden,jimenez2023shortcuts}, localised to late layers of probed encoders
\citep{pedersen2026probes} and mitigated by prevalence-equalised recalibration, which needs the artifact label at test
time \citep{kina2026prevalence}. These works treat an artifact's presence; none treats its location relative to the ROI
as a variable.
\paragraph{Removing shortcuts} Reweighting and GroupDRO \citep{sagawa2020groupdro}, last-layer retraining
\citep{kirichenko2023dfr} and linear concept erasure \citep{ravfogel2020inlp,belrose2023leace} need artifact labels or
paired data; erasure from unpaired labels removes label-correlated signal when the concept is correlated with the
label. Task-preserving erasure (SPLINCE; \citealp{splice2025}) and projection of biased directions in vision--language
models \citep{chuang2023debiasing} need concept labels or prompts. Random erasing and occlusion augmentation
\citep{zhong2020random,fong2019occlusions} use overlays as training noise, and test-time selection
\citep{bissoto2023tts} steers dermoscopy models with user keypoints. Counterfactual invariance
\citep{veitch2021counterfactual} motivates the remedy we recommend.
\paragraph{Foundation models} Classifiers trained on frozen foundation-model features inherit shortcut-like
behaviour that pooled multi-institutional evaluation can hide \citep{germani2026aggregation}, and shortcut testing
\citep{brown2023shortcut} probes whether performance gaps stem from encoding a sensitive attribute. We ask where in
the image the shortcut sits and what masking can and cannot remove.

\section{Problem setup and protocol}\label{sec:setup}
Let $Y\in\{0,1\}$ be the diagnosis and $A\in\{0,1\}$ the presence of an artifact. A \emph{trap} trains with
$P(A{=}1\mid Y{=}1)=0.9$ and $P(A{=}1\mid Y{=}0)=0.1$ and tests on a correlated environment with the same rates,
a \emph{reversed} environment with the rates swapped, and a clean environment in which the artifact is independent of
the label. A model that uses $A$ gains on the correlated test and collapses on the reversed one; the primary metric is
reversed-test AUROC, and clean AUROC measures the cost of a mitigation. The overlap
$r=|\mathrm{artifact}\cap\mathrm{ROI}|/|\mathrm{artifact}|$ is the variable of interest. Three designs vary it:
\emph{controlled sweeps} paste a synthetic artifact at overlaps 0--100\% on artifact-free images; \emph{real traps}
compare images whose real artifact lies inside the ROI ($r\ge0.5$, Trap~A) or outside it ($r<0.1$, Trap~B), each added
to one shared artifact-free group; the \emph{real-artifact transplant} pastes one real artifact instance inside
($r\ge0.95$) or outside ($r=0$) the ROI of the same artifact-free images. The \emph{location crossover}
$[\text{mask}-\text{ERM}]_{\text{out}}-[\text{mask}-\text{ERM}]_{\text{in}}$ of reversed-test AUROC summarises each
design. Unless stated otherwise backbones are frozen and linear heads are fitted; regularisation strength and the
decision threshold (balanced accuracy) are selected on clean validation data only. Splits are grouped by lesion or
patient identifier where published and otherwise by perceptual hash (and frame blocks).

\paragraph{Statistics} Uncertainty is a paired \emph{crossed} bootstrap: training seeds (or cross-validation folds)
are resampled as clusters, each test image receives one Poisson weight shared by every cluster in which it appears,
and AUROC differences are computed inside each cluster (10,000 replicates unless stated). \emph{Every interval of a
model comparison in the paper and the supplement is a crossed-bootstrap interval}, computed from regenerated per-image
predictions; the per-seed bootstrap of the original protocol, which treats a test set shared by the seeds as several
and gave intervals a median 1.56 times narrower, is not used (Supplement~S15). Agreement statistics between label
sources, which involve no training seeds, use an image bootstrap, and seven secondary analyses in the supplement come
from archived runs without per-image predictions and are reported as point estimates, marked as archived. Each family
of tests is Holm-corrected.

\paragraph{Registration} Every confirmatory analysis was registered in a document committed before its results; the registry with
commit hashes and times is in Supplement~S1. The real traps, sweeps and unaltered-data tests were registered first (the
16-test primary family was grouped afterwards); the matched traps, transplant, paste-edge control and operating points
were designed after the real-trap results and registered before their own results; each later registration was
pushed to GitHub before its analysis was run. Analyses decided after their data were seen are labelled
exploratory.

\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:limits}
\input{sections/discussion}

\section{Conclusion}
ROI masking is not a neutral preprocessing step. It removes shortcuts that live outside the ROI and leaves---or
amplifies---those that live inside it; moving the same real artifact across the ROI boundary of the same images
reproduces the effect, a two-parameter account predicts it, and it holds across masking implementations, encoders and
new patients. On unaltered clinical data the cost falls on the cases in which the in-ROI artifact points to the wrong
diagnosis: hidden in the overall AUROC, visible on those cases, and for a fine-tuned thyroid model partly beyond the reach
of threshold re-tuning. Audits of masked models should report artifact location relative to the ROI and performance on
shortcut-conflicting cases; where artifacts may lie inside the ROI and image-level artifact labels exist, a
class-conditional constraint on the masked features should be used instead of masking alone.
